tools.name: mcp__8dd1f51a-ea67-45bd-9826-32d43cc850bd__firecrawl_scrape
tools.description: Scrape one URL and return its content, or execute catalogued Alexandria capabilities. URL mode returns markdown by default, or HTML, links, screenshots, branding data, a targeted answer, or JSON matching a supplied schema, plus page metadata. Firecrawl may serve recently indexed content; set `maxAge: 0` for a live fetch. A successful response does not by itself confirm the page is still current. A named browser profile loads saved session data without saving changes to it. `firecrawl_search` with `sources` unset and `firecrawl_find_tools` can discover providers for the same fields across several pages; a matching Alexandria provider returns typed records in one call. Alexandria mode: `alexandria` selects catalogued capability execution and is mutually exclusive with `url`. Alexandria execution is billed at the capability's listed price and needs a team with Alexandria enabled.

alexandria.description: Catalogued Alexandria capability invocation, mutually exclusive with url. One {provider, capability, options} object or an array of 1-10, with contracts available through firecrawl_search or firecrawl_find_tools. Each call may include version to pin a published workflow; omitting it uses latest. Only requestId and timeout are supported alongside alexandria. The selected contract marks required inputs and any requiresOneOf groups (at least one member per group); it may include example.request/example.response and response.key (which may differ from records). Where pagination is declared, its fields govern paging with the same filters; catalogue next is separate from provider pagination. Returns per-capability results in data.alexandria with data, records, or an error with a code; individual capabilities can fail even when the outer response succeeds. Requires an API key on a team with Alexandria enabled. Some providers require accepted terms; blocked requests return the applicable requirements.

capability.description: Capability address as returned by search or discover, e.g. "series/observations".

version.description: Optional published workflow version. Omit to use the latest version.

options.description: Capability options as declared by its contract.

toolDetail.description: URL mode only: domain discovery detail, summary by default; compact returns provider/capability/description, full includes contracts. Ignored with alexandria.

tools.name: mcp__8dd1f51a-ea67-45bd-9826-32d43cc850bd__firecrawl_search
tools.description: Search web and specialized indexes, returning ranked results with query-relevant highlights. Each web result is a title, URL, and description. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. `includeDomains` and `excludeDomains` are mutually exclusive hostname filters; categories limit result types to `research`, `pdf`, `developer`, or `gov`. For a programming question, add `categories: ["developer"]`. It searches an index of public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation, and returns the results in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`. For a legal or regulatory question, `categories: ["gov"]` returns results in `data.web` with `category: "gov"` and cannot be combined with other categories; `firecrawl_gov_search` is the dedicated tool. Verify gov results' issuer, jurisdiction, status, and version before citing current law. Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. Returns result groups in `data` and an operation `id`.

highlights.description: Return query-relevant page excerpts for web and news results when available (default). Highlights appear in web `description` and news `snippet`; otherwise, original snippets are returned. Set to false to keep the original search snippets.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a background-task chip you previously created with spawn_task.

Call this when a suggestion you flagged is now stale, superseded, or irrelevant — e.g. you (or the user) already fixed it in this session, or you spawned a better-scoped replacement. To replace a chip: call spawn_task with the new suggestion first, then dismiss the old task_id.

Only chips the user hasn't acted on can be withdrawn from the queue. If the user already started or dismissed the task, the result says so (a dismissed task's copy kept for later is withdrawn too) — do not retry.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__spawn_task
tools.description:
Flag an out-of-scope issue for a separate background task.

Call this when you notice something worth fixing that would bloat the current change — dead code, stale docs, missing coverage, a confirmed TODO, or a security issue spotted in passing. Don't flag vague code-smell observations, trivial fixes you can do inline, or low-confidence hunches. A chip appears for the user; one click spins it off into its own session. Your current turn continues uninterrupted.

The prompt must stand alone — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation.

The result includes a task_id; call dismiss_task with it if the suggestion later becomes stale.

title.description: Under 60 chars. Imperative action phrase (start with a verb), e.g. "Fix stale README badge", "Remove dead config option". Shown as the chip label and the spawned session title.

prompt.description: The initial message for the spawned session. Self-contained — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation. Not shown directly in the UI.

tldr.description: One or two plain-English sentences shown on the suggestion card under the title. Lead with why you are suggesting this now — name what you noticed in this session — then say what the new session will do. Keep it readable: no file paths or code.

cwd.description: Optional. Absolute path to a different project root than the current session's — a path on the host this session runs on. The spawned session gets a fresh worktree under this path. Defaults to the current project — only set this when the work clearly belongs in another repo on that host.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

name.description: Tool name (e.g. computer, navigate, find, form_input, read_page). browser_batch cannot be nested. A tabs_create's new tabId is only returned when the batch ends — load that tab in a later call.

input.description: That tool's input — same shape you'd pass when calling it directly. For computer items whose action is left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key or type, and for form_input items, include action_summary in the item's input, as you would when calling that tool directly.

actions.description: List of tool calls to execute sequentially. Example: [{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"left_click","ref":"ref_12"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"type","text":"hello"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"screenshot"}}]

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

## Apify

Apify is the world's largest marketplace of tools for web scraping, data extraction, and web automation.
These tools are called **Actors**. They enable you to extract structured data from social media, e-commerce, search engines, maps, travel sites, and many other sources.

## Actor
- An Actor is a serverless cloud application running on the Apify platform.
- Use the Actor's **README** to understand its capabilities.
- Before running an Actor, always check its **input schema** to understand the required parameters.

## Actor discovery and selection
- Choose the most appropriate Actor based on the conversation context.
- Search the Apify Store first; a relevant Actor likely already exists.

1	# Design choices that measurably improve web and enterprise-software agents (2024-2026), with a focus on small/fast models
2	
3	Scope note: numbers are success rate (SR) in percent unless stated, always with benchmark and model. "pp" = percentage points. Several 2026 items are arXiv preprints found through a paper index; I read the relevant passages but did not check peer-review status. Statements under "Inferences" are mine, not measured results. All sources are paraphrased.
4	
5	Target system recap (for the report writer): one LLM loop per website, accessibility-style text with numbered controls, long pages cut at a character limit, 1-2 sentence thought plus up to 8 actions per turn, last 2 turns verbatim, no scratchpad (persistence only by filing pages as evidence), Qwen3.8-Flash-Next without thinking, a cheap decision model (Clef) available, 20-minute budget, unseen websites at evaluation.
6	
7	## 1. Observation and action space: pruning, alignment, actions per turn, diffs
8	
9	### Takeaway
10	Reshaping the observation and action space is the largest measured, training-free lever: AgentOccam went from 16.5 to 43.1 on WebArena with interface changes alone, and for most open-weight models a compact accessibility tree beats richer HTML by 5-19 pp. Blind multi-action batches were neutral-to-negative on enterprise UIs, while batches that re-observe between sub-steps (compound actions) and per-action change reports help.
11	
12	### Cited Findings
13	- AgentOccam incremental ablation, WebArena 812 tasks, GPT-4-Turbo: vanilla 16.5 -> remove rarely useful actions (noop, tab ops, go_forward, goto, hover, press) 25.9 (+9.4) -> disable scroll and pass the whole page 31.7 (+5.8) -> strip redundant text/formatting from the tree 37.1 (+5.4) -> replay selected elements of earlier pages as history 38.2 (+1.1) -> self-managed plan tree (branch/prune) with selective page replay 43.1 (+4.9). — [AgentOccam](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.13825)
14	- Same paper, mechanism: models scroll up and down when they do not know what to do, which delays tasks and causes loops; removing scroll and giving the full page fixed that (largest gains on GitLab 24.4 -> 35.0 and Reddit 33.0 -> 52.8). Average steps per task: 6.2 vanilla, 13.3 after action pruning, 8.6 after adding history, 9.0 final; observation tokens per step rose from about 2,210 to about 2,930. — [AgentOccam](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.13825)
15	- AgentOccam added two workflow actions, `note` (record key observations for later conclusions; used 194-219 times across the benchmark) and `stop [answer]`. Adding hand-written task strategies from SteP on top lowered SR from 43.1 to 41.1; adding an LLM judge that picks among all candidate actions raised it to 45.7. — [AgentOccam](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.13825)
16	- Multi-action per step, BrowserGym GenericAgent ablation: on WorkArena (enterprise ServiceNow) enabling multi-action moved GPT-4o 45.5 -> 40.6, Llama3-70B 20.0 -> 17.6, GPT-3.5 8.5 -> 9.4; on MiniWoB it moved 68.2 -> 68.5, 59.8 -> 63.0, 41.3 -> 41.4. Standard errors are about 2 pp, so each delta is within 1-2 SE; the tuned best configuration for all three models had multi-action off. — [WorkArena](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.07718)
17	- Same ablation, weaker models: adding long action descriptions cost Llama3 2.4 pp on WorkArena and 4.3 pp on MiniWoB; the authors conclude extra prompt features overwhelm weaker models. Dropping the visible-element tag cost Llama3 4.2 pp on WorkArena. Screenshot plus set-of-marks on top of the text tree gave only very minor gains for GPT-4o. — [WorkArena](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.07718)
18	- Accessibility tree vs HTML, WorkArena L1, AgentLab, 15-step cap: switching a11y -> HTML helps frontier models (GPT-5.1 high 55.8 -> 73.3, Claude Sonnet 4.6 52.4 -> 67.0) and hurts open models (gpt-oss-20b high 46.4 -> 27.6, gpt-oss-120b high 46.7 -> 38.8, Llama-3.1-70B 18.2 -> 3.6, Qwen3-VL-235B-Thinking 45.0 -> 39.8, Qwen3-VL-30B-Thinking 33.2 -> 26.1; Qwen3-VL-30B-Instruct 22.7 -> 25.5 is the exception). Input size: about 6.7k tokens (a11y) vs 56.7k (HTML). — [Read More, Think More](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.01535)
19	- Same paper, error analysis: under longer inputs weaker models produce more "not found" errors, i.e. they act on element ids that do not exist; a stronger model or a larger thinking budget suppresses this. — [Read More, Think More](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.01535)
20	- Page diffs and observation history, WorkArena L1, a11y: adding the last 4 pages raised SR by +0.3 to +10.9 pp across models (gpt-oss-20b low 20.0 -> 23.9; gpt-oss-120b low 33.6 -> 37.6; gemini-2.5-flash small budget 28.5 -> 39.4). Adding only the diff from the previous step over 9 steps gave similar gains (gpt-oss-20b low 24.2, high 49.1 vs 46.4 baseline) at about 13.7k input tokens instead of 39k for full history. — [Read More, Think More](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.01535)
21	- Agent-E (WebVoyager 73.2%, GPT-4-Turbo, text-only) attributes its result to three things: a planner/navigator split, task-dependent DOM distillation (text only, input fields only, or all interactive fields, keeping parent-child structure), and "change observation", where every action returns what changed in the page (for example that a popup with given elements appeared), implemented with a DOM mutation observer. No ablation isolates each part. — [Agent-E](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.13032)
22	- WebChallenger, open-weight GLM-4-32B, WebArena-lite 165 tasks, full system 58.8: removing the observation pipeline (skim per-section summaries, expand only relevant sections, long tables filtered in chunks) costs 17.6 pp and raises tokens per prompt from 1,850 to 8,793; removing compound actions (search, dropdown, form-fill workflows that handle intermediate state changes with sub-calls) costs 9.7 pp and raises average steps from 7.2 to 9.85; removing site memory costs 7.6 pp. Reported totals with open-weight models: 56.3 WebArena, 70.9 WorkArena, 51.0 Online-Mind2Web. — [WebChallenger](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.10423)
23	- Learned page contextualisation, WorkArena 165 tasks: raw observation -> same-model rewrite -> trained contextualiser: Llama-3.1-8B 1.2 -> 7.3 -> 37.0; Llama-3.1-70B 26.1 -> 29.1 -> 40.0; GPT-4o 38.2 -> 43.0 -> 44.2. On WebShop the untrained same-model rewrite hurt GPT-4o (34.8 -> 26.2) and Claude 3.5 Sonnet (26.6 -> 12.4). — [LCoW](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.10689)
24	- BrowserGym's prompt tooling warns that truncating a prompt from the end tends to cut crucial content and instead shrinks components in priority order (older history first, then the page from the bottom). — [BrowserGym ecosystem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.05467)
25	- Browser Use documents a default cap of 5 actions per step, with the batch executing only until the page changes; its fast mode drops the evaluation, next-goal and thinking fields and keeps only the memory field. (Read through an automated page summary, so wording of the defaults should be re-checked before relying on it.) — [Browser Use docs](https://docs.browser-use.com/customize/agent/all-parameters)
26	- Browser Use self-reports 89.1% on WebVoyager (586 tasks after removing 55, GPT-4o, default evaluator plus manual relabelling of failed/unknown cases); an independent re-evaluation on Online-Mind2Web measured the Browser Use agent at 26% (31% when allowed to use Google). — [Browser Use report](https://browser-use.com/posts/sota-technical-report); contradicted in magnitude by [Online-Mind2Web](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.01382)
27	
28	### Inferences
29	- The target system already uses the representation that favours small models (compact text tree with numbered controls). One caveat: the only non-thinking Qwen variant tested (Qwen3-VL-30B-Instruct) was the exception, scoring 2.8 pp higher with HTML, a difference that is probably within noise on 330 tasks; it does not justify switching. The remaining observation risk is the hard character cut: the evidence (AgentOccam full-page +5.8 pp, WebChallenger section skim -17.6 pp when removed, BrowserGym's truncation warning) says cutting silently is worse than an outline with expandable sections.
30	- "Up to 8 actions per turn" combined with "clicks controls that no longer exist" matches two measured effects: blind multi-action was not helpful on enterprise UIs, and weaker models hallucinate ids on long inputs. The low-cost fix is the Browser Use rule (stop the batch as soon as the page changes) plus a harness check that every referenced id exists in the current snapshot, returning a specific error. Batches remain useful for same-page form filling.
31	- A per-action change report is cheap to build from two consecutive snapshots (controls added/removed, dialog opened, URL changed) and is the common element of Agent-E's design and the diff result above.
32	- Removing idle actions from the menu (AgentOccam removed noop and scroll) suggests that aimless browsing while waiting should be handled by harness-side waiting, not by giving the model a wait-and-browse option.
33	
34	### Gaps
35	- No study measured exactly 8 actions per turn or the stop-on-change rule; the multi-action evidence is one 2024 ablation with deltas inside 1-2 SE.
36	- No ablation isolates Agent-E's change observation.
37	- I did not retrieve primary sources for VisualWebArena set-of-marks ablations, Skyvern, OSWorld-Verified or Agent S2/S3 within the time budget.
38	
39	## 2. Memory: notes, plans across steps, workflow memory, summarised vs raw history
40	
41	### Takeaway
42	An explicit, persistent memory beats relying on past reasoning text, and append-only entries beat a note that is rewritten each turn; action history is indispensable, while replaying past thoughts is mixed and can lock in early mistakes. Small Qwen models cannot be trusted zero-shot to write a memory that replaces raw context, so notes should supplement recent pages and the harness should write the mechanical parts.
43	
44	### Cited Findings
45	- Append-only vs overwrite memory, WebArena-Lite, Qwen 3.5 9B/27B, RL-trained, 5 runs: explicit overwrite memory beats reasoning+action history by 4.41 pp; append-only memory beats overwrite by a further 4.09 pp (9B) and 2.05 pp (27B). Overwrite memory lost recorded facts on later rewrites (example: the first of two matching reviewers was dropped when the second was seen) and lost error feedback within about four steps; after a rejected action the overwrite agent repeated it 1.95 times on average vs 1.29, and repeated it six or more times in 15.4% of cases vs 3.3%. — [AMBER](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07118)
46	- Same paper, zero-shot caution: untrained Qwen 3.5 9B scored 34.22 with full context but 21.82 when forced to rely on its own step-wise memory, i.e. it does not write compressed memory reliably without training. — [AMBER](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07118)
47	- History flags, BrowserGym GenericAgent: removing action history cost Llama3-70B 11.5 pp on WorkArena (20.0 -> 8.5) and GPT-3.5 3.3 pp. Replaying past thoughts cost GPT-4o 3.1 pp and GPT-3.5 5.5 pp on WorkArena, with the authors observing that agents then stick to early, even wrong, decisions and self-correct less; for Llama3 it helped slightly (+1.2 pp WorkArena, +7.6 pp MiniWoB). — [WorkArena](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.07718)
48	- Training-free trajectory summarisation, WebVoyager, Qwen3-VL-32B: baseline 57.8 (215k tokens/task) -> per-step self-summary replacing raw history 64.9 (73k tokens) -> plus retrieved cross-task hints 74.0. For Claude 3.7 Sonnet the summary alone was neutral (72.0 -> 72.9) and for Claude Sonnet 4 slightly negative (80.5 -> 79.7). In the summary, dropping action records hurt most (64.9 -> 54.7). Raw history window: 1 step 51.6, 3 steps 56.0, 5 steps 57.8, 7 steps 52.2. — [M2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.00503)
49	- Same paper: with the summary the agent sometimes takes more steps, which the authors read as persistence (it stops judging tasks impossible too early). On Online-Mind2Web medium tasks Qwen3-VL-32B went 30.2 -> 52.5. — [M2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.00503)
50	- Planning plus memory buffer for information-seeking, AssistantBench, GPT-4-Turbo: SeeAct 4.1 accuracy with a 15.5% answer rate -> SPA (adds a plan it can revise and a memory buffer that carries facts between steps) 11.1 accuracy, 35.9% answer rate, precision 26.3 -> 30.9. — [AssistantBench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.15711)
51	- Agent Workflow Memory, WebArena, GPT-4, online induction from the test stream: 35.5 vs 23.5 for the BrowserGym baseline (51.1% relative), with 5.9 vs 7.9 steps; Mind2Web cross-task step SR 45.1 vs 36.2. Abstract sub-routines beat retrieved concrete trajectories (+4.0 step SR over Synapse), text and code formats performed about the same, and gains appear after roughly 40 tasks on a site. — [AWM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.07429)
52	- Small-model scaffolding, AppWorld, Qwen3-8B: a summariser that must keep critical artifacts verbatim plus a history-isolated corrector raised task completion from 5.4 to 8.9 (FP16) and 3.0 to 5.9 (4-bit); context-length failures disappeared. The difference is not statistically significant on 168 tasks. — [Three Roles, One Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.11465)
53	- Abstract-only data points: a native Qwen computer-use agent keeps up to 20 recent screenshots and folds older history in blocks; a residual-memory method reports fewer repeated tool outputs and tool errors for Qwen3.8-27B on BrowseComp. — [Qwen-CUA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02352); [REMORY](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11287)
54	
55	### Inferences
56	- The observed "parrots its previous thought" matches the measured thought-history effect. The lowest-risk change is to stop showing earlier thoughts verbatim and show each earlier turn as action -> result lines, which every ablation above identifies as the essential part of history.
57	- A notes field is well supported, but the form matters: append-only short entries (fact found with where, scope checked, action that failed and why). A single field the model rewrites each turn is the variant that lost evidence and error feedback in AMBER.
58	- Because zero-shot Qwen wrote poor compressed memory, keep the last two raw turns and let the harness write the mechanical ledger (URLs, folders, pages and queries visited, errors) deterministically; the model only appends findings.
59	- Workflow induction (AWM) and cross-task hint banks need tens of prior tasks on the same or similar sites, which a single 20-minute run on unseen sites does not have. Low priority here; generic interaction hints are the only transferable piece and must not encode anything from the public sites.
60	
61	### Gaps
62	- No zero-shot, training-free comparison of append-only vs rewritten notes; AMBER's agents are RL-trained.
63	- No measurement of how much history Qwen3.8-Flash specifically should see; the best window in the one Qwen study (5 raw steps) used screenshots.
64	
65	## 3. Planning: plan-then-act, subgoal checklists, ledgers vs plain ReAct
66	
67	### Takeaway
68	Explicit planning helps when it is revised from observations and hurts when it is static, hand-written for other sites, or produced by an untrained planner for a capable executor. For a latency-bound small model the supported form is a lightweight progress ledger with stall-triggered replanning, not a planner call every step.
69	
70	### Cited Findings
71	- Plan-and-Act, WebArena-Lite, Llama-3.3-70B: ReAct executor without planner 9.85 (untrained) / 36.36 (fine-tuned). An untrained planner raises the untrained executor to 14.21 but drops the fine-tuned executor to 17.16. With a trained planner, replanning after every step adds 10.31 pp over a static plan (to 53.94), and reasoning traces add 4.36 pp (57.58). A fine-tuned 8B model with reasoning (53.33) matches the 70B without it (53.94). — [Plan-and-Act](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.09572)
72	- Magentic-One: the orchestrator keeps a task ledger (known facts, facts to look up, guesses, plan) and each turn fills a progress ledger (done? looping? progressing? next step?). A stall counter triggers reflection and replanning after more than two stalled turns. Replacing this with a plain next-speaker orchestrator lowers GAIA validation performance by 31% (GPT-4o). The authors note the fixed overhead helps long tasks and hurts short ones. — [Magentic-One](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.04468)
73	- AgentOccam's in-loop plan tree (plan edits are ordinary actions, no extra call) added 4.9 pp and was used mainly to abandon a failed strategy and try another; hand-written SteP strategies on top reduced SR by 2.0 pp, helping templated shopping tasks and hurting tasks needing general skills. — [AgentOccam](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.13825)
74	- SteP reaches about 33 on WebArena with 14 human-written, WebArena-specific policies; AWM exceeds it without human workflows (35.5). WebPilot (tree-search planning, GPT-4o) is listed at 37.2. — [AWM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.07429); [Plan-and-Act](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.09572)
75	- Tree search over real environment states: GPT-4o 18.9 -> 26.4 on VisualWebArena and 15.0 -> 19.2 on WebArena; Llama-3-70B 7.6 -> 16.7 and 7.6 -> 10.1, using a search budget of 20 and backtracking. — [Tree Search for LM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.01476)
76	- Reasoning per step: chain-of-thought vs action-only 23.81 vs 14.76 (WebArena subset, open-weight base agent); a longer structured thought template (summarise, checklist, verify, backtrack, list candidates) gave 23.33, no gain. Removing chain-of-thought cost Llama3-70B 11.5 pp on WorkArena. Forcing longer per-step thinking changed the action only 15% of the time and plateaued; sampling several actions per step cost most and helped least; spending the same budget on more interaction steps helped most. — [Thinking vs. Doing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07976); [WorkArena](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.07718)
77	
78	### Inferences
79	- Keep the short thought; do not expand it into a long template and do not add a planner call per step. An extra call per step roughly doubles latency, and the measured gains from separate planners come from trained planners.
80	- The transferable pieces are (a) a short list of facts still required, derived by the model from the brief at the start of each site and shown every turn, and (b) a harness stall counter that forces a strategy change. Both mirror the Magentic-One ledgers without the multi-agent overhead.
81	- Tree search needs resettable state and many extra steps; it is unsuitable for a single 20-minute live run with stateful sites.
82	- I found no direct evidence for a separate cheap "next subgoal" call; the nearest evidence (untrained planner hurting a capable executor) argues against it.
83	
84	### Gaps
85	- No study of a cheap decision model choosing subgoals for a small navigator.
86	- SteP and WebPilot numbers come from comparison tables in other papers, not their primary sources.
87	
88	## 4. Search and coverage: exploring scope and reformulating before concluding absence
89	
90	### Takeaway
91	The dominant failure of browsing agents on information-seeking tasks is stopping early or giving no answer, and accuracy rises with interaction effort; one forced re-check at the stopping point changes the decision about a quarter of the time. No paper measures a scope ledger for folders, tabs and pages directly.
92	
93	### Cited Findings
94	- AssistantBench, GPT-4-Turbo: accuracy is near zero for trajectories shorter than 5 steps or longer than 15 and peaks around 10. Not returning an answer accounts for 80% (SPA) and 97% (SeeAct) of errors; navigation errors (wrong path or loops) are 36.7% and 63.6% of errors. — [AssistantBench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.15711)
95	- The general BrowserGym agent scores at most 6.9% on AssistantBench against 27% on that leaderboard, which the authors attribute to it not being built for information retrieval. — [BrowserGym ecosystem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.05467)
96	- Mind2Web 2: the best system reaches up to 28% success vs 54% for humans. Incompleteness (information reported as not found, or fewer items than requested) is a leading agent error; systems not built for deep research terminate early. Partial completion rises with time spent, and pass-at-3 is clearly higher than single-run success. Hallucination affects at least 50% of tasks for all systems except the best (23%). — [Mind2Web 2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.21506)
97	- BrowseComp: GPT-4o with browsing 1.9%, o1 without browsing 9.9%, Deep Research 51.5%; accuracy scales smoothly with browsing effort; choosing among multiple attempts by self-reported confidence adds 15-25%. For questions it never solved, the model could usually find supporting evidence once given the answer, which the authors interpret as a lack of persistence and query reformulation rather than retrievability. Browsing models are badly calibrated (calibration error 82-91%). — [BrowseComp](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.12516)
98	- Check-again at the stop action, WebArena, open-weight agent: prompting once to re-inspect the page before finishing lengthens trajectories and raises SR in most domains; the agent changes its action about 25% of the time. Repeating the prompt several times starts to turn correct answers into wrong ones (the Maps domain dropped). — [Thinking vs. Doing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07976)
99	- Allowing the Browser Use agent to use a search engine on Online-Mind2Web raised SR only from 26% to 31%. — [Online-Mind2Web](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.01382)
100	
101	### Inferences
102	- "Searches one folder or one query and concludes" is the same early-termination pattern. Supported countermeasure: a single check-again gate when the agent wants to conclude absence or finish, fed with concrete, harness-collected facts (scopes opened, scopes seen in navigation but not opened, queries tried). One re-check only, since repeated re-checks degrade answers.
103	- A coverage ledger built from the agent's own actions and from navigation controls the page itself exposes (folder list, pager, tabs, filter state) keeps the model in charge of navigation while making unvisited scope visible. This generalises to unseen sites because it uses structure, not names.
104	- A minimum-effort rule before declaring absence (for example at least two scopes and two query formulations) is an inference from the short-trajectory result, not a measured intervention.
105	- Poor calibration means the agent's own statement that something does not exist should not be accepted as evidence; treat absence as a claim that needs the ledger to back it.
106	
107	### Gaps
108	- No ablation of coverage tracking, pagination handling or query-reformulation prompts in webmail/ERP-style interfaces.
109	- Deep-research agent papers were only covered through the two benchmarks above.
110	
111	## 5. Verification: self-critique, judges, read-back
112	
113	### Takeaway
114	Automatic judges for web trajectories agree with humans roughly 75-87% of the time, have high recall but under 70% precision, and are easily swayed by the agent's own reasoning, so they are useful as a single retry trigger grounded in the final state, not as an authority. Wrongly rejecting a correct result is more damaging than wrongly accepting one.
115	
116	### Cited Findings
117	- Pan et al.: evaluators that see the final state and the action list agree with the WebArena oracle 80.6% (GPT-4V end-to-end), 82.1% (captioner + GPT-4), 74.4% (captioner + Mixtral, open weights) and 68.0% (Qwen-VL-chat end-to-end). Used as the signal for up to three retry rounds, they raise a GPT-4 agent's WebArena SR by 29% relative (GPT-4V judge) or 16% (open-weight judge) from a 15.6 baseline, at about 46.7 steps per task versus 5.9 for AWM. — [Autonomous Evaluation and Refinement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.06474); [AWM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.07429)
118	- Same paper: false negatives hurt more than false positives, because forcing a retry of an already successful run almost always ends in failure. Giving the judge earlier states did not help, and the captioner is not shown the task, to stop it describing things that are not on the page. — [Autonomous Evaluation and Refinement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.06474)
119	- AgentRewardBench (1,300+ expert-annotated trajectories): no LLM judge exceeds 70% precision. GPT-4o judge 69.8 precision / 83.1 recall; Qwen2.5-VL 64.3 / 89.8; Llama 3.3 67.7 / 79.0. Official rule-based checks have 83.8 precision but 55.9 recall. For a GPT-4o-mini judge, accessibility tree only gives recall 86.1, screenshot only gives the best precision 64.5, and both together are worse than screenshot alone. — [AgentRewardBench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.08942)
120	- Same paper, judge failure modes: accepting the agent's claim of success when nothing was done, and missing a detail of the instruction (the item was found but not purchased). Loop detection by the judge had 78-92% precision but 17-59% recall. — [AgentRewardBench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.08942)
121	- WebJudge: extract key points from the task, select relevant screenshots, then judge; agreement with humans 83.6% (GPT-4o), 85.7% (o4-mini), 87.0% (fine-tuned Qwen2.5-VL-7B). It deliberately ignores the agent's final message because that message often contains hallucinations. Judging each key point separately is better with three or fewer key points (87.9 vs 86.1) and worse with more (76.3 vs 81.4). — [Online-Mind2Web / WebJudge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.01382)
122	- A judge that chooses among several candidate next actions added 2.6 pp on WebArena (43.1 -> 45.7, GPT-4-Turbo), motivated by the agent hastily committing to a poor option. — [AgentOccam](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.13825)
123	- A history-isolated corrector on Qwen3-8B nearly halved parameter/schema errors (17.8% -> 9.5% of failures) but removed the few successes on the hardest tasks, where it lacked context. — [Three Roles, One Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.11465)
124	- BrowserGym lists failing to notice an unsuccessful submission and wrongly formatted entries as a standard error class. — [BrowserGym ecosystem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.05467)
125	
126	### Inferences
127	- For the bid form, compare what the form actually contains (re-read from the rendered page after filling) against the case-file records in code, and show the model only the mismatches. Exact value comparison does not need a judge, and judges are the weak link.
128	- Use the cheap decision model for narrow, evidence-bound yes/no questions on the final state (for example whether a confirmation is visible), with a few key points, never on the agent's own summary, and with text or screenshot rather than both.
129	- Allow at most one corrective pass before signing; treat a judge "no" as a prompt to re-inspect, not as a verdict, because false negatives are the costly error.
130	
131	### Gaps
132	- I found no measured study of reading values back after form filling.
133	- No public evaluation of the Clef decision model was looked up.
134	
135	## 6. Misleading content inside pages: prompt-injection and distractor findings
136	
137	### Takeaway
138	Telling an agent to ignore misleading content has little or no effect and defensive prompts cost task utility, whereas changing what the model is shown (removing, delimiting, structuring) and restating the task after the content do measurably help. Distractors that are relevant to the task and placed next to the real target are the most effective ones.
139	
140	### Cited Findings
141	- Pop-up attacks, OSWorld and VisualWebArena: agents click adversarial pop-ups 86% of the time on average and task SR falls by 47%. An instruction to ignore pop-ups left the click rate unchanged (93.3 -> 95.9, OSWorld screenshot agent); a more specific version reduced it to 52.0. A blank pop-up was clicked 2.4% of the time; emptying the pop-up's alt text cut the rate from 91.8 to 68.1, while keeping the text and adding an advertisement notice only reached 77.1. A hook phrased as the user's own task got 62-93%; a generic virus alert got 1.1% on the text-plus-marks web agent. — [Attacking Vision-Language Computer Agents via Pop-ups](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.02391)
142	- WASP, real web apps: agents begin following injected instructions in 17-86% of cases; attackers complete their goal in at most 16%. A defensive system prompt cut GPT-4o's hijack rate from 0.32 to 0.17 but lowered benign utility from 0.595 to 0.459, and did nothing for GPT-4o-mini (0.345 -> 0.333, utility 0.432 -> 0.351). Putting page content in the lowest-privilege message role did not help. Task-related injections worked about three times as often as generic ones (0.226 vs 0.071, GPT-4o). — [WASP](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.18575)
143	- AgentDojo, GPT-4o: no defence, utility 69.0 / attack success 57.7; delimiting tool output as data 72.7 / 41.7; repeating the user's task after each tool output 85.5 / 27.8; injection classifier 41.5 / 8.0; restricting tools to those needed 73.1 / 6.8. Phrasing mattered greatly: a generic "ignore previous instructions" got 5.4% while a message addressed to the model by name got 57.7%. — [AgentDojo](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13352)
144	- Environmental injection: injected elements that mirror the genuine target and sit next to it leak data in up to 70% of steps; defensive system prompts did not counter it. — [EIA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.11295)
145	- Benign distraction: with no adversary, agents are still pulled off task by pop-ups, recommendations, search results and chat content; the pop-up scenario produced the most unfaithful actions, and reducing the perception burden changed how often the agent stayed on task. — [Caution for the Environment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.02544)
146	
147	### Inferences
148	- A decoy label inside a genuine record is the "task-relevant distractor next to the target" case, the hardest one in these studies. Prompt rules alone are unlikely to fix it; a rendering change is the supported direction.
149	- Rendering rule: show each record with a harness-built header of structural metadata (where it was found, list-row fields such as sender, date, status, revision, reference) followed by the body inside explicit delimiters marked as quoted page content. Judge a record's status from the header and from comparison with sibling records; treat labels inside the body as describing that section only.
150	- Restate the task and the current subgoal after the page text in every turn. This is the cheapest measured improvement here (utility 69.0 -> 85.5 in AgentDojo) and is independent of site.
151	- The observed over-distrust of the right message is consistent with the measured utility cost of defensive prompting. Having trap warnings from 29 rules in every navigation prompt may itself cause rejections; moving acceptance decisions out of the navigator (file with a doubt tag, decide later) avoids relying on the navigator's suspicion.
152	- Popups and access checks: handle dismissal structurally where the page exposes a close control, and report it in the change line, rather than relying on an instruction to ignore them.
153	
154	### Gaps
155	- All cited work studies injected instructions or advertisements, not misleading status labels, superseded revisions or look-alike records; the mapping to those traps is my inference.
156	- No study measures metadata-first rendering.
157	
158	## 7. Small models specifically: what transfers, what does not, Qwen-family results
159	
160	### Takeaway
161	Interface-level fixes (compact observation, action history, short reasoning, summarised history, mechanical-error guards) transfer to small open models and often help them more than frontier models; richer observations, self-written memory that replaces context, long prompts and untrained planners do not.
162	
163	### Cited Findings
164	- Transfers: compact tree over HTML (open models +5 to +19 pp, Qwen3-VL included); chain-of-thought (Llama3-70B +11.5 pp WorkArena); action history (+11.5 pp); observation history or diffs (gpt-oss-20b +2.7 to +4.2 pp); self-summarised history (Qwen3-VL-32B +7.1 pp and 66% fewer tokens, neutral for Claude); section-skim observation (GLM-4-32B +17.6 pp); mechanical-error correction (Qwen3-8B, schema errors halved). — [Read More, Think More](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.01535); [WorkArena](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.07718); [M2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.00503); [WebChallenger](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.10423); [Three Roles, One Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.11465)
165	- Does not transfer or is risky for small models: HTML and screenshots (gains concentrate in frontier models); extra prompt features and long descriptions (hurt GPT-3.5 and Llama3); untrained same-model page rewriting (mixed, harmful on WebShop); memory that replaces context without training (Qwen 3.5 9B 34.2 -> 21.8); untrained static planners with a capable executor (36.4 -> 17.2). — [Read More, Think More](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.01535); [WorkArena](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.07718); [LCoW](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.10689); [AMBER](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07118); [Plan-and-Act](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.09572)
166	- Qwen results: Qwen3-VL on WorkArena L1 with the text tree scores 45.0 (235B thinking), 33.2 (30B thinking) and 22.7 (30B instruct, no thinking). — [Read More, Think More](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.01535)
167	- Qwen results: Qwen3-VL-32B on WebVoyager 57.8 -> 74.0 with summarised history plus retrieved hints, above an unaided Claude 3.7 Sonnet agent (72.0). — [M2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.00503)
168	- Qwen results: fine-tuned QwQ-32B in a planner/executor setup reaches 48.15 on WebArena and 81.36 on WebVoyager (text only). — [Plan-and-Act](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.09572)
169	- Qwen results: Qwen2.5-VL as agent is judged by humans at 33.3 on WebArena, 21.7 on VisualWebArena and 13.8 on WorkArena++ subsets; as a judge it has 64.3 precision and 89.8 recall. — [AgentRewardBench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.08942)
170	- Open vs closed gap on enterprise tasks, same generic agent: WorkArena L1 Claude 3.5 Sonnet 56.4, GPT-4o 45.5, Llama-3.1-405B 43.3, Llama-3.1-70B 27.9, GPT-4o-mini 27.0; on the compositional L2 level 39.1, 8.5, 7.2, 2.1, 1.3. — [BrowserGym ecosystem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.05467)
171	- After scaffolding removed mechanical failures for Qwen3-8B, reasoning/planning errors became the largest remaining class (26.4% -> 34.2% of failures). — [Three Roles, One Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.11465)
172	
173	### Inferences
174	- The 10 pp gap between the thinking and non-thinking Qwen3-VL-30B variants suggests that running without thinking has a real cost, but the Thinking-vs-Doing result says more interaction steps repay better than longer per-step reasoning. Keeping thinking off and spending the time on more, better-grounded steps is defensible.
175	- Since compositional enterprise tasks are where small models collapse, the harness should carry the composition (facts ledger, coverage ledger, required-facts list) and leave each model turn a local decision.
176	- Keep prompts short: every added rule competes with the page for a weak model's attention. A 29-rule brief in each navigator prompt is a candidate for trimming to the rules that affect navigation, with the rest applied at adjudication and form-fill time.
177	
178	### Gaps
179	- No web-agent result for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next was found; the nearest are Qwen3-VL, Qwen 3.5 and one abstract-level mention of Qwen3.8-27B.
180	- Most ablations on small models are from 2024-era Llama3 or GPT-3.5; transfer to a 2026 fast model is assumed.
181	
182	## 8. Ranked list: at most ten changes worth making in a few hours
183	
184	### Takeaway
185	Ordered by evidence strength multiplied by fit to the observed weaknesses and by ease of implementation: persistent append-only notes with a harness-written coverage ledger, safer action batching with change feedback, and separating "file" from "judge" come first. All ten are site-agnostic and leave navigation choices to the model.
186	
187	### Cited Findings
188	- 1. Append-only notes plus harness-written ledger, shown every turn. Add a notes output the harness appends (never rewrites): fact found and where, scope checked, action that failed and why; the harness adds visited URLs, folders, pages and queries itself. Keep the last two raw turns. Evidence: append-only beats rewritten memory by 4.1 pp and explicit memory beats reasoning history by 4.4 pp; untrained Qwen cannot replace context with its own memory (34.2 -> 21.8); a note action is part of the 43.1 AgentOccam agent; a memory buffer doubled the answer rate on AssistantBench. — [AMBER](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07118); [AgentOccam](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.13825); [AssistantBench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.15711)
189	- 2. Stop the action batch when the page changes, verify ids before executing, and return a change line per action. Lower the cap from 8 to about 3-5 except for same-page form fills. Evidence: blind multi-action was -4.9 pp (GPT-4o) and -2.4 pp (Llama3) on WorkArena; weaker models hallucinate ids on long inputs; Browser Use stops batches on page change with a cap of 5; re-grounded compound actions are worth 9.7 pp and fewer steps. — [WorkArena](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.07718); [Read More, Think More](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.01535); [Browser Use docs](https://docs.browser-use.com/customize/agent/all-parameters); [WebChallenger](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.10423); [Agent-E](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.13032)
190	- 3. File first, judge later. The navigator files every candidate that matches the reference on structural grounds with a one-line doubt tag; acceptance is decided afterwards with all candidates side by side (cheap decision model as a chooser over metadata). Evidence: false rejections are the costly error and are rarely recoverable; choosing among generated candidates added 2.6 pp; models verify better than they find (+15-25% from picking among attempts); rewritten memory dropped the first match when a second appeared. — [Autonomous Evaluation and Refinement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.06474); [AgentOccam](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.13825); [BrowseComp](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.12516); [AMBER](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07118)
191	- 4. Metadata-first, delimited rendering of records, and fewer trap warnings in the navigator prompt. Evidence: instructing agents to ignore content had no effect (93.3 -> 95.9) while removing or neutralising it did (2.4% for blank content); delimiting data raised utility and cut attack success (57.7 -> 41.7); defensive prompts cost 14-16 points of utility. — [Pop-up attacks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.02391); [AgentDojo](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13352); [WASP](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.18575)
192	- 5. One check-again gate before concluding absence or finishing, listing unopened scopes and untried query forms from the ledger. Evidence: a single re-check changes the action about 25% of the time and raises SR in most domains, repeated re-checks hurt; trajectories under 5 steps score near zero on information tasks; early termination is the leading agent error on long-horizon search. — [Thinking vs. Doing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07976); [AssistantBench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.15711); [Mind2Web 2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.21506)
193	- 6. Replace the hard character cut with an outline: section headings with counts, collapsed regions with ids, rows matching the reference kept, and an expand action. Evidence: full page instead of scrolling +5.8 pp; section skim worth 17.6 pp with a 32B open model; truncation from the end cuts crucial content. — [AgentOccam](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.13825); [WebChallenger](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.10423); [BrowserGym ecosystem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.05467)
194	- 7. History hygiene: do not replay earlier thoughts; show older turns as action -> result lines and add a short diff of the page against the previous turn. Evidence: thought history cost GPT-4o 3.1 pp and GPT-3.5 5.5 pp and made agents hold on to early decisions (slightly positive for Llama3); action history is worth 11.5 pp; diffs give history's gains at a third of the tokens. — [WorkArena](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.07718); [Read More, Think More](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.01535); [M2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.00503)
195	- 8. Stall detector and harness-side waiting. If the same action, same page or near-identical thought repeats twice, inject the fact and require a different scope or filing what exists; when the agent must wait, pause in the harness without model calls. Evidence: stall counter with replanning is part of the ledger design whose removal costs 31%; removing idle actions (scroll, noop) removed loops and added 5.8 pp; retained error feedback cut repeated invalid actions from 1.95 to 1.29 per event. — [Magentic-One](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.04468); [AgentOccam](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.13825); [AMBER](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07118)
196	- 9. Restate the task and current subgoal after the page text each turn, and keep a short model-written list of facts still required for this site. No per-step planner call. Evidence: repeating the task after tool output raised utility from 69.0 to 85.5; replanning from observations is worth 10.3 pp while a static plan from an untrained planner can halve a good executor; a long thought template gave no gain. — [AgentDojo](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13352); [Plan-and-Act](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.09572); [Thinking vs. Doing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07976)
197	- 10. Before signing, read the filled form back from the page, compare with the case file in code, show mismatches, allow one corrective pass; use the decision model only for narrow yes/no checks on the final state with one modality. Evidence: judges reach 80-87% agreement but under 70% precision and accept the agent's own claims; final-state evidence is sufficient; text gives recall, screenshots precision, both together are worse. — [AgentRewardBench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.08942); [Online-Mind2Web / WebJudge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.01382); [Autonomous Evaluation and Refinement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.06474)
198	
199	### Inferences
200	- The ordering is my judgement. Items 1, 2, 6 and 7 rest on direct ablations; items 3, 4, 5, 8, 9 and 10 combine a measured mechanism with an inferred application to this system.
201	- Mapping to observed weaknesses: parroting thoughts -> 7 and 1; one folder or one query -> 1 and 5; rejecting candidates -> 3; distrust from decoy labels -> 4 and 3; clicking vanished controls -> 2; aimless browsing while waiting -> 8.
202	- Rough effort: items 2, 7, 8 and 9 are harness-only edits under an hour each; items 1, 5 and 10 are one to two hours each; items 3, 4 and 6 touch rendering or the evidence pipeline and are two to three hours each.
203	- Not worth doing in this setting: tree search or multi-attempt voting (needs resets and many steps), a planner call per step, cross-task workflow induction, HTML or screenshots for the navigator, a longer structured thought template, more defensive wording, and judges that see both text and screenshot.
204	- Fair-play fit: every item keeps the model choosing where to go and what to search; the harness only records, re-displays, validates and compares. Item 6 must stay a rendering aid with model-chosen expansion, not a crawl. Any generic interaction hints must not contain values or names from the public sites.
205	
206	### Gaps
207	- None of the ten was measured on this stack (Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, text tree, four concurrent site agents); each should be checked with a before/after run, changing one item at a time.
208	- Interactions between items are untested, for example whether notes plus diffs plus a goal reminder lengthen the prompt enough to offset gains for a small model.

9	## 1. Tail latency: what do hedged requests, tied requests, adaptive timeouts and retry budgets recommend, and what timeout and hedge delay fit a call with p50 = 3 s and p95 = 9 s?

11	### Takeaway

142	- Simple repetition baselines can beat complex agents at lower cost, so redundancy should be compared against "just call it again". — [Kapoor et al., AI Agents That Matter](https://agents.cs.princeton.edu/)
143	- Search summary only. A reviewer-gated loop that samples candidates one after another and stops at the first one the reviewer approves outperformed verifier and critic variants at every budget while using far fewer samples; evaluated with Qwen-family agents and a trained reviewer. — [SWE-Review, arXiv 2607.06065](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2607.06065)
144	
145	### Inferences
146	- Independence is the test. Two samples of the same model on the same page text share the model, the prompt and the input, so they share most errors. Three ways to de-correlate, cheapest first: deterministic checks (types, ranges, units, totals, cross-record consistency), which share nothing with the model; a different view of the input (table-structured text versus raw text, or a different chunk order); a different model for the second opinion (the cheap decision model for yes/no questions, a frontier model as tie-breaker).
147	- Dual extraction with comparison fits this system well. Extraction is one call per page, it runs in parallel, and only pages that feed the bid matter. Run a second extraction with a varied prompt view on those pages, compare field by field in code, and send only disagreeing fields to a third opinion. Own estimate of cost: one extra call per bid-relevant page (perhaps 15-40 calls on a 200-260 call run), near zero added wall time when run in parallel under the cap.
148	- The "am I done" decision is the second good place: BATS shows un-checked agents stop too early. A code-side checklist of required record types, plus a cheap yes-probability from the decision model on "does this page contain X" before filing or discarding a document, covers it for a few short calls.
149	- Racing a second agent from a different start is a portfolio strategy: it helps when run times are heavy-tailed and failures depend on the starting path (see question 5). Under a cap of 32 it should use capacity that is free anyway: when one site agent finishes early, start a second agent on the site that is furthest behind, entering by search where the first entered by navigation, and let both write to the same record store.
150	- Voting on every navigation step triples the call count for a 0-2 point gain and is not worth it under a call cap. Disagreement between two cheap proposals can instead be used as a trigger to spend more (a verifier call) at forks that matter.
151	- The signature path is a different kind of redundancy: the action must happen once, so the calls leading to it can be sent in duplicate from the start (hedge delay zero), but the side effect (requesting the one-time code, submitting) must stay single and idempotent in code.
152	
153	### Gaps
154	- No source measures dual extraction with comparison on web pages for typed records; the benefit estimate rests on the general correlation results.
155	- The 60 % same-wrong-answer figure is from one multiple-choice dataset; correlation for free-form extraction is unknown.
156	- Whether the cheap decision model's errors are independent of Qwen's on this content is unknown and can only be measured on saved pages.
157	
158	## 5. Restart and recovery: checkpoint and restart with a summary, supervisor timeouts, "restart beats continue", and preserving what was learned
159	
160	### Takeaway
161	A stalled or looping agent should be stopped by a supervisor and restarted with a fresh context that contains only a code-built summary of facts found, pages visited and dead ends; the evidence says a failed attempt left in the context makes the next one worse, and restart theory says cut-offs help exactly when run times are heavy-tailed, as they are here.
162	
163	### Cited Findings
164	- Background. For algorithms with heavy-tailed run times, restarting improves expected run time; with a known distribution a fixed cut-off is optimal, and without that knowledge Luby's universal schedule is within a logarithmic factor of optimal (Luby, Sinclair and Zuckerman 1993). — [Runtime Distributions and Criteria for Restarts, arXiv 1709.10405](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1709.10405)
165	- Context contamination: when a failed attempt stays in the context window, later attempts run at a higher per-step error rate. Fitted to SWE-bench Verified, the error-rate ratio after a failure was 7.1, and a model that assumes independent retries overestimated pass@3 by 17.4 points (98.6 % versus 81.2 %). The paper proves that clearing the context before a retry reduces the attempts needed, and derives an optimal attempt length for a fixed total budget. Abstract only; single-author preprint, not peer reviewed as far as I could see. — [Yang 2026, Why Retrying Fails, arXiv 2605.08563](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.08563)
166	- BATS replaces the raw trajectory with a summary of key steps, findings and failure causes whenever it continues or pivots, and refreshes the trace every 10 iterations, keeping a checklist whose entries are never deleted. — [Liu et al. 2025, arXiv 2511.17006](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.17006v1)
167	- Search summary only. A Luby-style campaign of 15 fresh sub-runs with conversation reset, in LLM-driven heuristic search for process control, reached a higher median (35.1 versus 33.5) but a lower best score (51.6 versus 55.5) than 52 ad-hoc independent runs, in about 4.1 hours instead of about 36. — [arXiv 2603.20537](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.20537)
168	- Search summary only. Sequential resampling gated by a reviewer (stop at the first approved candidate, at most K attempts) beat verifier and critic variants while using fewer samples. — [SWE-Review, arXiv 2607.06065](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2607.06065)
169	- Tree-search agents with backtracking exist for software tasks (Monte Carlo tree search with iterative refinement); I did not extract numbers. — [SWE-Search, arXiv 2410.20285](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.20285)
170	- Trajectories of the same agent diverge early and the divergence compounds (search summary only), and in one study 18.8 % of tasks had diverged by step 2. — [arXiv 2608.13867](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.13867); [Mehta 2026, arXiv 2602.11619](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11619)
171	- Background. Latency-induced probation: take a slow component out of service and readmit it when it recovers. — [The Tail at Scale, summary](https://blog.acolyer.org/2015/01/15/the-tail-at-scale/)
172	
173	### Inferences
174	- The observed failure "one agent looped until the deadline" is a heavy tail in time-to-completion: most runs finish a site in 5-8 minutes and a few never do. That is the condition under which a cut-off plus restart lowers expected time. With one known good-run duration, a fixed cut-off is the right form: restart an agent that has produced no new record or filed page for about 60-90 s, or that repeats the same action three times (own estimate of the thresholds; a normal step takes 3-9 s, so 75 s is 8-20 steps of nothing).
175	- Restart with a clean context and a summary built by code, not with the old transcript. The summary holds: records already filed, URLs visited, searches tried, and what led nowhere. This follows both the contamination result and the BATS design, and it keeps the rule that the model chooses the navigation.
176	- Vary the restart: a different entry point (site search versus menu navigation), a slightly higher temperature, or a reworded goal. A restart that replays the same start with the same prompt at low temperature tends to re-enter the same loop.
177	- Preserve learning outside the agent: the record store and the visited-URL set live in the orchestrator and are written at every step, so a restart, the cut-off, or a process crash loses nothing. Writing the store to disk after each stage also allows the submission stage to be retried without re-investigating.
178	- Limit restarts to two per site and stop restarting once the investigation window has under about 60 s left; a restart costs roughly 5-15 calls of re-orientation (own estimate).
179	- A restart is also the cheapest answer to an agent whose context has grown long: fewer input tokens per call means lower latency per step.
180	
181	### Gaps
182	- I found no controlled experiment comparing "continue" with "restart with summary" for web navigation agents; the direct evidence is from coding agents, a theoretical model and one industrial search study.
183	- No published guidance on stall thresholds for web agents; the 60-90 s and three-repeat values are my estimates and should be set from logs of good runs (longest gap between two filed pages in a run that scored 100).
184	- The contamination paper was read as an abstract only.
185	
186	## 6. Determinism: temperature, seeds, prompt caching and ordering; does a lower temperature reduce harmful variance for navigation?
187	
188	### Takeaway
189	Temperature 0 and a fixed seed reduce variance but do not make hosted models deterministic, and no study shows that lowering temperature fixes navigation failures; use low temperature for extraction and form filling, accept variance in navigation, and control it with budgets, verification and restarts.
190	
191	### Cited Findings
192	- Five models, eight tasks, ten runs per condition at temperature 0, top-p 1 and a fixed seed: accuracy varied by up to 15 % across runs, and the gap between best-possible and worst-possible accuracy reached 70 % (72 points for Mixtral on college math in the table). Raw-string agreement over 10 runs ranged from 0 % to 86 %; parsed-answer agreement from 12 % to 99.6 %. — [Atil et al. 2024, arXiv 2408.04667](https://arxiv.org/html/2408.04667v5)
193	- Same paper: longer outputs are less stable (output length correlates negatively with agreement); a locally run model without serving optimisations was deterministic, so the authors suspect continuous batching or prefix caching on hosted endpoints; they suggest limiting maximum generation tokens. — [Atil et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2408.04667v5)
194	- Agents: in a small ablation (20 questions, 5 runs) the number of distinct action sequences generally rose with temperature; Claude and Gemini were near-deterministic at temperature 0 (1.0 sequences) while Llama still produced 2.3 and GPT-5 still diverged, so temperature alone does not explain inconsistency. — [Mehta 2026, arXiv 2602.11619](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11619)
195	- Search summary only. At temperature 0 the standard deviation of SWE-bench Verified pass@1 stayed above 1.5 points, attributed to infrastructure nondeterminism. — [arXiv 2608.13867](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.13867)
196	- Search summary only. A tool-calling study reports that greedy decoding at temperature 0 does not fully activate the knowledge needed for correct tool use and that parallel sampling at higher temperature improved results; not a web-navigation setting. — [arXiv 2606.10875](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.10875)
197	- A strong budget-aware search agent ran its acting model at temperature 0.7 and used temperature 0.0 only for answer selection and judging. — [Liu et al. 2025, arXiv 2511.17006](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.17006v1)
198	- Explanations given by practitioners: batched GPU arithmetic depends on what else is in the batch, requests are routed to different hardware, and mixture-of-experts routing can depend on batch context; none of this is controllable through API parameters. Blog-level sources. — [Towards AI, June 2026](https://pub.towardsai.net/the-mirage-of-determinism-at-temperature-zero-0f3992d0d0e1); [Label Studio](https://labelstud.io/learning-center/how-to-handle-non-determinism-in-agent-evaluation/)
199	- The BrowserGym ecosystem records benchmark version, package versions, commit hash and timestamps per study because results otherwise do not reproduce. — [BrowserGym ecosystem, arXiv 2412.05467](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.05467)
200	
201	### Inferences
202	- Split the settings by call type. Extraction and form filling have one right answer: temperature 0 to 0.2, a seed if the proxy accepts one, structured output, a tight `max_tokens`. Navigation and search are exploration: keep the provider default or a moderate value, because determinism there mainly makes a bad path repeatable.
203	- Diversity is useful on purpose in two places: the second opinion in dual extraction, and a restarted or racing agent. Those calls should differ from the first (prompt view, entry point, slightly higher temperature).
204	- Keep the start of every prompt byte-identical across calls (system text, tool descriptions, fixed instructions first; changing content last). If the proxy caches prefixes this lowers latency; it also removes one source of run-to-run difference. Sort any lists that are fed to the model (links, records) so the order does not depend on arrival time of parallel tasks.
205	- The dominant variance in the team's runs is wall-clock (hangs, loops), not token-level. Even a perfectly deterministic model would have produced the bad runs, because the proxy's timing differs each time and timing changes which facts arrive before the cut-off.
206	
207	### Gaps
208	- No controlled comparison of temperature settings for web navigation agents was found, and nothing on Qwen3.8-Flash-Next specifically (seed support, prompt caching through this proxy, default sampling settings).
209	- Ordering effects of parallel tool results on agent behaviour: I found no quantitative source; the advice to sort inputs is a precaution.

211	## 7. Which concrete measures can be added to the existing Python asyncio system in a few hours, with expected benefit and cost?
212	
213	### Takeaway
214	Eight measures, ordered by expected benefit per hour of work: bounded and hedged model calls behind one concurrency governor, a start-up canary, a live deadline controller with an anytime bid, a stall-and-loop supervisor that restarts with a summary, redundancy only at extraction and at the "done" decision, and a measurement harness with fault injection. In a normal run they add roughly 15-25 % model calls and no wall time; in a bad run they are the difference between a full signed bid and a partial one.
215	
216	### Cited Findings
217	- Hedge after the 95th percentile for about 5 % extra load; cancel the loser. — [Dean and Barroso 2013](https://cacm.acm.org/research/the-tail-at-scale/)
218	- At most three attempts per request and a retry budget of about 10 % of requests; retry at one layer only; shed low-criticality work first. — [Google SRE book](https://sre.google/sre-book/handling-overload/)
219	- For LLM calls, time the hedge on the first token, cap hedges at 5-10 % of traffic, and be careful behind a shared rate limit. — [InfoQ](https://www.infoq.com/articles/adaptive-hedged-requests-p99-latency/); [Tian Pan](https://tianpan.co/blog/2026/05/02/tail-tolerant-retry-policy-llm-gateway-latency-cliff)
220	- A per-step budget block with tiers changes agent behaviour; verification of each constraint and summary-based context refresh add further gains. — [Liu et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.17006v1)
221	- Clear the context before a retry. — [Yang 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.08563)
222	- Same-model repeats share errors; agreement is a better doubt signal than a vote. — [Kim et al. 2025](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v267/kim25e.html); [Mehta 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11619)
223	- Measure reliability over repeated trials (pass^k) and under injected faults. — [tau-bench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.12045); [ReliabilityBench](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.06112v1)
