# Deterministic control shells make runs repeatable

The spread from 10 to 100 on identical code is a timing and control problem, not a model-capability problem, and the evidence says to fix it with deterministic structure around the model, not with more prompting, more agents or more reasoning. Three of the seven recorded runs reached 100, so Qwen3.8-Flash-Next without thinking can do the task; what changed between runs was which calls hung, which facts arrived first, and whether an agent entered a loop that the harness only warned about. Five remedies carry the weight, in descending order of evidence: bound each model call at 20 to 30 seconds and send one backup request after about 8 seconds, where the code now waits 120 to 150; stop replaying the agent's own thoughts, refuse repeated no-effect actions, and restart a stalled agent in a clean context seeded from a code-built ledger; stamp every question and conclusion with the input values it rests on, so that a correction reopens it, wakes its owner and is announced as a change; gate "absent" and "done" on a harness-recorded coverage ledger with exactly one forced re-check; and hold a signable bid at all times behind a protected submission reserve. Published ablations credit structural changes of this kind with 15.6 points on one multi-agent system and 31% of performance on another, against 5 to 9 points for prompt rewording, and a benchmark shows models repeating a failed action unaware in 23% to 59% of cases even with the repetition visible in context. An LLM orchestrator, a planner call per step, tree search, voting on navigation, LLM-written history summaries, extra trap warnings and thinking mode for navigation are each unsupported for small models, too slow for a 20-minute window, or measured to hurt. Every recommended change leaves navigation, searches and document choice to the model and keys only on structure (page fingerprints, fact kinds, input hashes), so it carries over to websites with other names, layouts and information splits. None has been measured on this stack, so the report grades each claim and ends with a build order and a fault-injection test that proves the mechanisms faster than scored runs can.

## Three runs at 100 prove capability; timing and control decide the rest

The team's record, as given in the research brief, is three runs at 100 and four between 10 and 45 from one code version. That distribution is bimodal, which points to run-level events (a site lost to a loop, a fact that landed after the cut-off, a hung call that ate two minutes) and not to gradual quality loss. The largest published failure study of multi-agent LLM systems reaches the same reading: across more than 1,600 annotated traces from seven frameworks, **system-design issues account for 44.2% of failures, with step repetition the single largest mode at 15.7%**, followed by reasoning-action mismatch at 13.2% and unawareness of termination conditions at 12.4% ([MAST](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.13657v3)). The same study measured what repairs buy: refined prompts moved one system from 25.0 to 34.4 and another by about 5 points, while a topology change with an objective check reached 40.6, and its authors conclude that structural changes beat prompt changes without resolving every mode ([MAST](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.13657v3)). Magentic-One's ablation agrees from the other side: removing its ledgers, progress tracking and loop detection costs **31% of performance** on GAIA validation ([Magentic-One](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.04468)).

The determinism lever is already spent. `starter-kit/llm.py` runs every Qwen call at temperature 0, and the literature says that neither removes variance nor cures navigation failures: at temperature 0 with a fixed seed, accuracy across ten repeats still varied by up to 15% on hosted models ([Atil et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2408.04667v5)), and the same agent on identical inputs produced 2.3 to 4.2 distinct action sequences in ten runs, with consistent tasks reaching 82-87% accuracy and inconsistent ones 41-65% ([Mehta 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11619)). Greedy decoding has a second cost: the original ReAct error analysis suspected it as the reason a model regenerates its previous thought and action and cannot leave the loop ([ReAct](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03629)). A near-identical prompt yields an identical turn, so a loop at temperature 0 is stable, and a warning string that is itself identical every turn becomes part of the repeated pattern.

Fan-out arithmetic explains why hangs reach almost every run. A component that is slow once in 100 requests makes a 100-way fan-out slow 63% of the time ([The Tail at Scale, summary](https://blog.acolyer.org/2015/01/15/the-tail-at-scale/)); by the same arithmetic a run of 200 to 260 model calls with a 1% hang rate contains at least one hang in about 93% of runs, and each hang currently costs one agent up to 120 to 150 seconds. The table maps the five observed failure causes to the remedy the evidence supports best. "Strong" means a direct ablation or several independent systems with a mechanism that matches the failure; "moderate" means a measured mechanism whose application here is inferred; "weak" means a design inference with no measurement.

| Failure in the bad runs | Best-supported remedy | Nature of the evidence | Strength |
|---|---|---|---|
| Model calls that hang | Per-attempt cap from logged latency, one backup request at the rolling p90, loser cancelled, start-up canary | Classic tail-latency practice; one simulation and engineering posts for LLM calls; no peer-reviewed LLM study | Strong for the cap, moderate for the backup request |
| Agents that loop or repeat | No replay of own thoughts; refusal of repeated no-effect actions keyed on page state; stall counter; clean restart from a code-built ledger | Ablations on history and action space; loop benchmarks on Qwen-family models; ledger ablation; source code of four production detectors | Strong that warnings are insufficient and structure helps; moderate for the exact ladder |
| Acting on facts since corrected | Input-basis stamp on every question and conclusion; level-triggered wake; explicit CHANGED line; old thoughts dropped on change | A belief-update benchmark; classic truth maintenance; no measurement of push versus re-reading in LLM teams | Moderate |
| Facts that arrive late | Blocked, tentative and ready states; superset filing on the stable attribute; survey budget then hold; bid recomputed on every new record | Prerequisite gating in planner-compiler systems; nothing published on gating by input stability | Weak to moderate |
| Searches that cover too little | Harness-written coverage ledger with unopened scopes; one check-again gate on "absent" and "done"; outline in place of truncation | Early-termination findings on three benchmarks; a single re-check measured; the ledger itself unmeasured | Moderate |

## A short cap and one backup request erase the two-minute hang penalty

The current client waits `WARM_TIMEOUT = 120` seconds for a navigation call and `CALL_TIMEOUT = 150` for an extraction call, then retries in sequence up to five times with backoff; `ask_clef` in `starter-kit/models.py` waits 120 seconds with no retry. Tail-latency practice says this is the wrong shape for a deadline. A hedged request goes out only after the first has been outstanding longer than the 95th-percentile latency and the first answer wins, which limits extra load to about 5% ([The Tail at Scale, summary](https://blog.acolyer.org/2015/01/15/the-tail-at-scale/)). Google's overload rules cap a request at three attempts, hold retries under 10% of a client's requests, and retry at one layer only; without that budget worst-case load grows about threefold, with it about 1.1-fold ([Google SRE book](https://sre.google/sre-book/handling-overload/)). The difference for a slow model call is structural: sequential retry delivers primary plus retry, hedging delivers the faster of the two ([Tian Pan](https://tianpan.co/blog/2026/05/02/tail-tolerant-retry-policy-llm-gateway-latency-cliff)). In a 50,000-request simulation with 5% stragglers, **hedging at the observed p90 cut p99 latency by about 74% for 8.9% extra requests**, and the same article warns that for streaming endpoints the timer must run on the first token, and that hedging behind a shared rate limit can itself trigger throttling ([InfoQ](https://www.infoq.com/articles/adaptive-hedged-requests-p99-latency/)). No peer-reviewed study measures hedging of LLM API calls; this evidence is classic systems work plus engineering posts.

The team's own numbers make the case sharper than the literature does. Navigation calls run at a median of 3 seconds and a 95th percentile of 9, and in one bad run 9 of roughly 148 attempts never answered. The research team's own lognormal fit to those two percentiles (a calculation, not a published result) puts the 99th percentile near 14 seconds and the share of healthy calls above 30 seconds at 0.03%, so a call silent at 30 seconds is hung, not slow. Their Monte Carlo of one agent's 65 sequential calls at a 6% hang rate gives a median model wait of about 780 seconds under the current policy, 363 with a 30-second cap, 325 with a 20-second cap and 266 to 277 with one backup request sent after 7 to 9 seconds, for 5% extra calls on a healthy day and up to 22% on a bad one. Almost all of the gain comes from the cap; the backup adds the rest and, unlike a very short cap, never discards a primary that is slow but alive.

That last property matters because the code records why the timeouts are long: a model scaled to zero answers its first call slowly, a 75-second timeout once cut off a legitimate first turn with a large prompt under load, and extraction calls with thinking on take longer than navigation calls. The change therefore has four parts. Send one backup after the rolling p90 of that call type (start at 8 seconds for thinking-off steps), keep the primary running, take whichever answers first and cancel the other. Set the per-attempt cap per caller label from logged latency, starting at 30 seconds for navigation steps and at the logged 99th percentile for thinking-on extraction, and cut attempts from five to three. Run three parallel one-token calls at start-up as a canary and warm-up, and list every model the agent relies on in `agent.json` so the platform waits for it. Apply the same bounds to Clef. One governor should own concurrency: a semaphore below the shared limit of 32, agent steps ahead of the extraction fan-out, and at most four slots for backups. `MAX_CONCURRENT` is 16 today because test runs may overlap; during the final evaluation no second run of the team should be active, since hedging helps with independent hangs and makes self-inflicted queueing worse. Two facts remain unknown and each takes ten minutes to test: whether a client-side cancel frees the proxy's concurrency slot, and whether the proxy streams, which would let a "no first token" timer separate hung calls from long answers.

### The signature is the one step that must never be late

An unsigned bid scores nothing and a signed partial bid scores its filled positions, which is the textbook case for an anytime design: keep a valid, submittable bid from the first complete record set onward and improve it until a hard start-of-submission time. Three changes follow. Recompute the deterministic bid whenever the case file changes, so the cut-off, a restart or a crash never loses work. End the investigation the moment no required fact is missing; `Team.hook` in `starter-kit/agent.py` currently finishes only when every agent is idle and no extraction is pending, which is the correct quiescence test for work in transit ([Dijkstra-Scholten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dijkstra%E2%80%93Scholten_algorithm)) but waits for agents that have nothing left to find. Keep `submit_reserve` at 480 seconds for now: the notes propose a live reserve with a floor near 330 seconds, but the code's own comment records a run that ended unsigned with 330, so the floor should drop only after fault-injected runs sign with margin.

Budget prompts deserve less than their popularity suggests. Appending used and remaining budget after every tool result let an agent match a tenfold larger budget at **31.3% lower cost** and added about two points on BrowseComp, but the study used Gemini 2.5 and Claude Sonnet 4, counted tool calls instead of seconds, and mainly stopped agents from quitting early ([Budget-aware tool use](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.17006v1)). The loop already prints `TIME LEFT` each turn. For a small model whose failure is looping until the deadline, the budget has to be enforced in code: a step allowance per open question, after which the supervisor parks the question and moves the agent on.

## Refusals and clean restarts end loops that warnings leave running

Repetition in language models is self-reinforcing: the more often a sentence already appears in the context, the more likely it is generated again ([Xu et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.02369)), and agents imitate the pattern of action-observation pairs in their context even after it stops being useful ([Manus](https://manus.im/blog/Context-Engineering-for-AI-Agents-Lessons-from-Building-Manus)). Small instruct models are the worst case. On WebShop, **Qwen3-4B-Instruct spent 36.7% of its actions in loops** against 5.7% for the 30B instruct variant and 0.2% for Gemini 2.5 Flash, and action entropy is low on loop steps, so the agent is confidently fixated ([TIDE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.02196)). Visibility of the repetition does not break it: with three or six repeats of an invalid action in the history, models repeated it unaware in **22.7% to 59.1%** of snapshots, 35.1% for Qwen2.5-7B ([MIRAGE-Bench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.21017)).

The present history format feeds this mechanism. `Agent._messages` in `starter-kit/worker.py` replays every past assistant reply, thought included, and shortens only the user turns, so a looping agent reads many copies of its own stale sentence and one copy of the corrected fact. The ablation evidence points the other way: on WorkArena, replaying past thoughts cost GPT-4o 3.1 points and GPT-3.5 5.5 points, with agents observed holding on to early wrong decisions, while removing the action history cost Llama3-70B 11.5 points ([WorkArena](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.07718)). Collapsing all but the last five observations beat full history by 3 points on SWE-bench Lite ([SWE-agent](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.15793)), and a page diff against the previous step gave the gains of full observation history at about a third of the tokens ([Read More, Think More](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.01535)). The first change is therefore the cheapest one in this report: show older turns as harness-written action and result lines, never as the model's own thought, and collapse repeated attempts into one ledger line with a count and an outcome, which keeps the failure visible, as Manus recommends, while removing the repeated pattern.

The second change replaces advice with refusal. Every shipping detector whose source the notes read uses similar thresholds and a soft response: OpenHands nudges at three identical erroring calls and halts at four ([OpenHands SDK](https://github.com/OpenHands/software-agent-sdk/blob/main/openhands-sdk/openhands/sdk/conversation/stuck_detector.py)), Gemini CLI injects feedback after five identical tool calls ([Gemini CLI](https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/blob/main/packages/core/src/services/loopDetectionService.ts)), and Browser Use adds escalating messages at 5, 8 and 12 repeats while stating that it never blocks an action ([Browser Use](https://github.com/browser-use/browser-use/blob/main/browser_use/agent/views.py)). The existing loop does the same: after the third identical turn it appends a fixed sentence. The measured wins come from hard structure. SWE-agent's linter rejects an invalid edit, says it was not applied and shows the current state, for 18.0% against 15.0% resolved, and without recovery one failed edit drops the chance of eventual success from 90.5% to 57.2% ([SWE-agent](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.15793)). AgentOccam's largest gains came from removing the actions a lost model overuses, 16.5 to 25.9 on WebArena from action pruning and a further 5.8 from disabling scroll, and the pattern held for the small Gemini-1.5-Flash ([AgentOccam](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.13825)). The guard that follows has a gate before each action, which refuses a click or fill whose target is no longer the element the model saw and refuses any action that has already brought nothing new twice on the same page fingerprint; the refusal is written as an environment result that opens with NOT EXECUTED, names the action, the count and the current page, and never repeats verbatim. Keying the block on action plus page state is what keeps legitimate repetition, such as pressing Next through a list, free.

The third change is escalation, because a refusal alone turns 78 wasted clicks into 78 refusals. Magentic-One's counter is the model to copy: it rises on a stalled round, decays by one on a good round, and at three triggers a replan in which every agent's context is cleared and re-seeded from the ledger ([AutoGen source](https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/blob/main/python/packages/autogen-agentchat/src/autogen_agentchat/teams/_group_chat/_magentic_one/_magentic_one_orchestrator.py)). Here the progress signal can be deterministic, which none of the cited systems can offer: a turn counts as progress when a fact slot was filled, an open question closed, or evidence with a new content hash was filed. Restart theory backs the reset, since cut-offs lower expected run time exactly when run times are heavy-tailed ([Restart criteria](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1709.10405)), and one preprint, read only as an abstract, fits a 7.1-fold higher per-step error rate when a failed attempt stays in context ([Yang 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.08563)). Magentic-One also documents the cost: agents rediscover sub-task solutions after a reset ([Magentic-One](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.04468)). The restart must therefore carry over the tabu list, the coverage ledger and the dead ends in a handover built by code. `bounded()` in `starter-kit/agent.py` today restarts once, only when an agent ends unfinished, with a new `Agent` whose coverage record starts empty.

Who writes the handover is the one point where the notes' sources disagree. A per-step self-summary raised Qwen3-VL-32B from 57.8 to 64.9 on WebVoyager ([M2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.00503)), while LLM summarisation lowered Qwen3-4B-Instruct on all three tasks tested, 9.6 to 4.8 on WebShop ([TIDE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.02196)), and an untrained Qwen 3.5 9B fell from 34.22 to 21.82 when forced to rely on its own step-wise memory ([AMBER](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07118)). The effect depends on model size and no result exists for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, so a ledger written by code avoids the question. The least-evidenced rung is the forced choice at the second stall, in which the navigator proposes candidate actions without history, code removes refused ones, and Clef picks through its `choice` question type; no source measures it, so it goes in last. All thresholds (refuse at the third identical no-effect action, restart at three stalls, park the question after two restarts) are scaled from the cited systems, were exercised only against synthetic sequences, and produced two false positives in drafting that were fixed by qualifying turn keys with page state.

## Corrections must retract conclusions, and unstable inputs must gate work

The architecture should stay. One case file, one model loop per source and code that derives the open questions is a blackboard system in the classic sense, and the published evidence favours exactly this shape for dependent information gathering. Anthropic lists tasks with many dependencies between agents and domains where all agents need the same context as poor fits for its orchestrator-worker design, and notes that its lead agent cannot steer subagents while they run ([Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system)). A supervisor that rewords what sub-agents said loses information and spends more tokens ([LangChain](https://www.langchain.com/blog/benchmarking-multi-agent-architectures)). A blackboard on which helpers volunteer beat a master-slave controller by **13% to 57% relative** on data-discovery tasks, at about 1.8 times the cost ([Salemi et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.01285v2)), and across 260 configurations multi-agent setups ranged from +80.8% on decomposable work to -70.0% on sequential planning ([Kim et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.08296)). OpenAI's own guidance states that orchestration by code makes speed, cost and performance more predictable ([OpenAI Agents SDK](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/multi_agent/)). No source compares an LLM orchestrator with deterministic control on a task whose open questions are mechanically derivable; that deterministic control is at least as good here is an inference, and a safe one given that an orchestrator would add a serial three-second call to the critical path.

Stale beliefs are the failure this architecture does not yet handle. Showing the full case file every turn is not enough: on the STALE benchmark the best model scored **55.2%**, with a measured gap between retrieving the new evidence and acting on it ([STALE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.06527)), and Cognition's argument that every action embeds decisions other agents cannot see describes the stale rejection exactly ([Cognition](https://cognition.com/blog/dont-build-multi-agents)). Four properties of the code let an old value win. The corrected value appears only inside regenerated question text with no change marker; the agent's older thoughts restate the old value; `CaseFile.answer` closes a question by id, so an "absent" given under old inputs survives the correction; and `Team.hook` wakes an idle agent only for a question id it has not seen, so a changed question under an unchanged id wakes nobody. The remedy is truth maintenance in its minimal form: record what each conclusion depended on and retract it when a premise changes ([Reason maintenance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reason_maintenance)). Each question carries a hash of the input values it was derived from, each answer and give-up stores the hash it was made under and counts only while the two match, and the wake test becomes level-triggered: is there a question visible to this agent whose current basis it has not given up on. When a merge changes a basis, the affected agents get a CHANGED line with old value, new value and source, and their older thoughts are dropped. The two notes place that line differently, first in the briefing or after the page; the measured result favours the end of the prompt, since repeating the user's task after each tool output raised utility from 69.0 to 85.5 on AgentDojo ([AgentDojo](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13352)). No study compares push with per-turn re-reading in LLM teams, so the grade is moderate: the mechanism is measured, the fix is classical.

Late facts need a state that published systems lack. LLMCompiler dispatches a task as soon as its dependencies resolve ([LLMCompiler](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2312.04511)) and MetaGPT activates an action only after all prerequisites arrive ([MetaGPT](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.00352v7)), but neither models inputs that exist and may still be revised. The design answer is three states derived from the case-file schema: blocked (an input is missing, not shown), tentative (inputs present, an upstream question that can revise them still open) and ready. A tentative question carries a restricted contract, file every candidate that shares the most stable attribute and do not answer "absent" yet, so that a later correction costs zero turns because the deterministic matcher re-selects from what is already on file. Tying stability to the closure of upstream questions is order-independent, which a quiet-period timer is not, and arrival order is precisely what differed between the good and bad runs. An agent with nothing visible gets a bounded survey of about six turns and is then held; that cap is the deterministic end of the 45-turn blind search. Tentativeness should expire at about half the run so that an upstream question that never closes cannot block the bid.

Routing is where the unseen evaluation sites bite. `briefing()` shows every agent every open question, which survives any split of information but invites agents to search for facts their site cannot hold; narrowing by site name would fail the moment the split changes. The pattern that degrades safely keys on the kind of fact a question needs, a property of the bid rules, and learns the site-to-kind relation at run time: a model-written site card after a first look is the prior, the first record of a kind extracted from an agent's filing overrides it, and a question nobody advances within a lease of about 75 seconds widens until every agent sees it. Under a wrong profile the worst case is one or two leases of delay, never an invisible question. The supporting evidence is indirect. Volunteering after profiling beat central assignment in the blackboard study, unrestricted self-selection tripled token use for little gain in another ([LbMAS](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.01701)), and a single agent degrades sharply once two or more unrelated domains share its prompt ([LangChain](https://www.langchain.com/blog/benchmarking-multi-agent-architectures)). Whether a fast non-thinking model writes usable cards is unknown, so the router must work with none, every score starting at "unknown" and provenance taking over. An agent's "absent" then means "not on my site", a routing signal, and closes the question globally only when every plausible holder has disclaimed it.

## One re-check and a visible frontier widen searches on unseen sites

Searching one folder with one query and concluding is the dominant failure of browsing agents in general. On AssistantBench, accuracy is near zero for trajectories under five steps and not returning an answer accounts for 80% to 97% of errors ([AssistantBench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.15711)); on Mind2Web 2 the best system reaches 28% against 54% for humans, with incompleteness a leading error ([Mind2Web 2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.21506)); and on BrowseComp models usually found supporting evidence once handed the answer, which its authors read as a lack of persistence and reformulation, alongside calibration errors of 82% to 91% ([BrowseComp](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.12516)). An agent's own statement that something does not exist is therefore not evidence. The measured countermeasure is small: one prompt to re-inspect before finishing changes the action about **25% of the time** and raises success in most domains, while repeating it turns correct answers into wrong ones ([Thinking vs. Doing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07976)).

`starter-kit/coverage.py` already holds the right instrument, a harness-written record of pages opened, text typed and lists followed that gates "complete" and "absent" with at most two refusals. Two extensions close the remaining gap, and both are inferences because no paper ablates a coverage ledger. The gate should also apply once to `done`, and it should name the scopes that exist but were never opened, taken from the section list on the agent's own site card and from navigation controls the page exposes. Because those labels come from the model's reading of the site and from page structure, nothing is tuned to a website. The same reasoning argues against a hard truncation of long pages: `Tab.observe` cuts page text at 14,000 characters from the end, BrowserGym's tooling warns that truncating from the end tends to cut crucial content ([BrowserGym](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.05467)), passing the full page in place of scrolling was worth 5.8 points for AgentOccam, and removing a skim-then-expand observation pipeline cost an open-weight 32B model **17.6 points** ([WebChallenger](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.10423)). An outline with section headings, counts and a model-chosen expand action is the supported replacement; it must stay a rendering aid, since code that expands everything would be a crawl.

Three smaller findings shape what the navigator sees. The compact accessibility-style text is the right representation: switching to HTML helps frontier models and costs open ones 5 to 19 points at roughly eight times the tokens ([Read More, Think More](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.01535)). Memory should be append-only and mostly written by the harness, since append-only entries beat a rewritten note by 2 to 4 points in RL-trained Qwen agents, and overwriting lost the first of two matches when the second appeared ([AMBER](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07118)). And misleading content is best handled by rendering, not warnings: an instruction to ignore pop-ups left the click rate unchanged (93.3% to 95.9%) while blanking the content cut it to 2.4% ([Pop-up attacks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.02391)), a defensive system prompt lowered benign utility from 0.595 to 0.459 for GPT-4o and did nothing for GPT-4o-mini ([WASP](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.18575)), and delimiting tool output as data raised utility while cutting attack success from 57.7 to 41.7 ([AgentDojo](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13352)). That body of work studies injected instructions, not superseded revisions or look-alike records, so the mapping to this challenge's traps is an inference. It supports three moves: show each record with a harness-built header of structural fields followed by the body inside explicit delimiters, restate the open questions after the page text (the loop now places the briefing before it), and move acceptance out of the navigator. Filing every structurally matching candidate with a doubt tag and judging later, side by side, respects the finding that a false rejection is the costly and rarely recoverable error ([Pan et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.06474)) and that no LLM judge exceeds 70% precision on web trajectories ([AgentRewardBench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.08942)).

## Twelve popular ideas that cost minutes and buy nothing here

Each idea below is widely recommended and each fails one of the constraints: a small model without thinking, a 20-minute wall clock, live sites that cannot be reset, a shared cap of 32 calls, or evaluation on sites never seen.

| Popular idea | Why it does not pay here | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| LLM orchestrator or supervisor above the site agents | Adds a serial call and a relay layer; the open questions it would compute are already derived in code | Poor fit for many dependencies ([Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system)); relay loss ([LangChain](https://www.langchain.com/blog/benchmarking-multi-agent-architectures)) |
| Planner call every step, or a longer thought template | An untrained planner dropped a capable executor from 36.36 to 17.16; a structured template scored 23.33 against 23.81 for plain reasoning | [Plan-and-Act](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.09572); [Thinking vs. Doing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07976) |
| Tree search with backtracking | Needs resettable state and a search budget of about 20 per decision | [Tree Search for LM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.01476) |
| Voting or self-consistency on navigation steps | Majority vote over three runs gained 0 to 2 points; two models that are both wrong agree on the wrong answer about 60% of the time | [Mehta 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11619); [Kim et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07962) |
| Advisory loop nudges, or asking the model each round whether it is looping | Models repeat unaware in 23-59% of cases; a self-check costs a call per round and relies on the missing self-awareness | [MIRAGE-Bench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.21017) |
| LLM-written summaries that replace raw history | Lowered small Qwen models; positive only at 32B | [TIDE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.02196); [AMBER](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07118) |
| More trap warnings and defensive wording | No effect on behaviour, measurable utility loss; extra prompt features cost weaker models 2 to 4 points | [WASP](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.18575); [WorkArena](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.07718) |
| HTML or screenshots for the navigator | Open models lose 5 to 19 points with HTML at 56.7k against 6.7k tokens | [Read More, Think More](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.01535) |
| Workflow memory, hint banks, site-specific policies | Gains appear after roughly 40 tasks on a site; hand-written strategies lowered AgentOccam by 2 points; site knowledge also breaks fair play | [AWM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.07429); [AgentOccam](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.13825) |
| Thinking mode for navigation | Mixed on loops (the 4B thinking variant looped more on two of three tasks); more interaction steps repay better than longer per-step reasoning | [TIDE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.02196); [Thinking vs. Doing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07976) |
| An LLM judge as final authority, or repeated self-checks | Under 70% precision; forcing a retry of a correct result almost always ends in failure | [AgentRewardBench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.08942); [Pan et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.06474) |
| Lowering temperature | Already 0; hosted models stay non-deterministic and greedy decoding stabilises loops | [Atil et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2408.04667v5) |

The thinking-mode row carries the strongest counter-evidence and deserves a fair statement: on WorkArena the thinking variant of Qwen3-VL-30B scored 33.2 against 22.7 for the instruct variant ([Read More, Think More](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.01535)). The code comment in `agent.py` puts navigation without thinking at about twice the speed, and under a wall clock that doubling buys the extra steps the evidence says help more. Thinking stays on for extraction, where it already is, and is a reasonable experiment for a single post-stall call. Redundancy is worth its calls in exactly two places, both where copies fail independently and the result is checkable in code: deterministic validation plus a second extraction with a different view of pages that feed the bid, and Clef answering narrow yes-or-no questions about a final state. Agreement between runs is a better signal of doubt than a vote ([Mehta 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11619)).

## Build order: wall clock first, then history, then the case file

The order below multiplies evidence strength by fit to the observed failures and by cost. Effort figures are the research team's estimates and none of the changes has run on this code base; only the hedged-call wrapper and the loop guard were executed, against fake requests and synthetic action sequences.

| Order | Change | Where | Failure removed | Evidence | Effort |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Backup request at rolling p90, per-label cap, three attempts, one governor, canary, same bounds for Clef | `llm.py`, `models.py` | Hung calls | Strong / moderate | 2 h |
| 2 | Older turns as action-and-result lines without thoughts; deduplicated attempt ledger; open questions restated after the page | `worker.py` | Loops, stale beliefs | Strong | under 1 h |
| 3 | Basis stamps on questions and answers; level-triggered wake; CHANGED line; thoughts dropped on change | `casefile.py`, `agent.py` | Stale conclusions, missed wake-ups | Moderate | about 70 min |
| 4 | Gate before each action (stale target, tabu on page plus action), factual refusal, stall counter with decay | `worker.py` | Loops | Strong for refusal, moderate for thresholds | 1 to 1.5 h |
| 5 | Stall-triggered restart from a code-built handover that keeps tabu and coverage; at most two; then park the question | `agent.py` | A site lost to one agent | Moderate | 1 to 1.5 h |
| 6 | Finish when nothing is missing; bid recomputed on every case-file change; reserve held at 480 s | `agent.py` | Cut-off, thin bid | Moderate | 1 h |
| 7 | Tentative state, "absent" refused while tentative, survey budget then hold | `casefile.py`, `agent.py` | Late facts, blind search | Weak to moderate | 30 min |
| 8 | Coverage gate on `done`; unopened sections from the site card; one re-check only | `coverage.py` | Thin searches | Moderate | 1 h |
| 9 | Router keyed on fact kind: card as prior, provenance as posterior, lease widening | new `router.py` | Blind search; changed information split | Weak to moderate | 1 to 2 h |
| 10 | Outline with expand in place of the 14,000-character cut; header-plus-delimited record rendering | `browser_env.py` | Missed content, decoy labels | Moderate | 2 to 3 h |
| 11 | Forced choice through Clef at the second stall; dual extraction on bid-relevant pages | `worker.py`, `casefile.py` | Residual loops, silent extraction errors | Weak | 1.5 to 2 h |

With three hours, rows 1 and 2 fit and remove the largest wall-clock loss and the cheapest source of repetition; rows 3 to 5 are the next half day and cover the two failures that cost the most turns in the logs. Because the current version has already scored 100, each change belongs behind the `sanity.enabled(...)` switch the code already uses for `coverage_gate` and `agent_restart`, so that a regression can be turned off without a revert.

Scored runs cannot validate any of this in the time available. tau-bench showed that agents succeeding on single trials still fail repeated ones, with pass^8 under 25% in its retail domain ([tau-bench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.12045)), and the research team's exact binomial calculation puts the cost of separating 80% from 95% reliability at about 30 full runs; ten clean runs in a row still occur 10.7% of the time for an 80% system. The usable instruments are offline and per mechanism. A wrapper that makes 6% of calls hang, slows 10% threefold and stalls one agent for 90 seconds tests rows 1 and 5 on demand. Holding back one agent's extraction results by 60 to 120 seconds tests rows 3 and 7, and the final case file must match an undelayed run. Replaying recorded trajectories through the guard sets row 4's thresholds, and re-running extraction 20 times over pages saved from good runs gives a stage-level pass^k. The acceptance test before the final is three consecutive fault-injected runs that each sign a complete bid, with seconds of slack at the cut-off and at the signature logged as continuous metrics, because a shrinking margin is visible in one run and a pass rate is not.

## Conclusion

The research changes the question. The team asked which better approach would make a model-directed agent reliable, and the answer is that the approach in place, a blackboard with one model loop per site, is the one the evidence favours; what fails is that validity is not scoped to state. A model call is treated as worth waiting for long after its usefulness has expired, an action as valid after the page it was chosen on has gone, a conclusion as true after its inputs have changed, and "absent" as global when it was established for one folder. Each remedy here is the same move applied at a different layer: stamp the thing with the state it was valid under and let code retract it when that state changes. That is why the fixes transfer to websites nobody has seen, since a hash of input values, a page fingerprint and a latency percentile carry no site knowledge.

Two further implications follow. The best-evidenced changes subtract (old thoughts, repeated actions, long waits, premature closures), while the weakest add model calls (forced choice, dual extraction, site cards), so under a 32-call cap and a 20-minute clock the order of work is also the order of safety. And reliability at this level cannot be read off a leaderboard score before the final: the only claim the team can verify today is order-independence, that injected hangs, delays and corrections no longer change the signed bid. If that holds under fault injection, the remaining variance belongs to the model's reading of unfamiliar pages, which is the part the rules require a model to own.
